system.name: HongMeng
system.one_liner: a production microkernel (HM) that configures isolation strength per OS service to balance microkernel principles with performance and Linux compatibility

components.name: Apps
components.role: applications that invoke drivers, e.g., via ioctl

components.name: Device Manager
components.role: registers device file nodes for each driver container

components.name: Core Kernel
components.role: the trusted core kernel underlying apps and the VFS path

components.name: Virtual File System
components.role: exposes driver device nodes (e.g., /dev/a) and redirects invocations to the right driver container

components.name: Linux Driver Container
components.role: runs the Linux Runtime (DC-Base) hosting a reused Linux Driver, reached via IPC from the VFS

components.name: Linux Driver
components.role: a reused, unmodified Linux driver running inside the Linux Driver Container

components.name: DC-Base
components.role: driver container base providing redirected kthread/memory interfaces for the Linux runtime

components.name: Native Driver Container
components.role: houses the performance-critical Twin Driver on the native/fast path

components.name: Twin Driver
components.role: a rewritten twin of a performance-critical driver that handles I/O IRQs on the fast path while the control plane stays in the Linux Driver Container

content.key_idea: HM's device manager registers each reused driver as a VFS file node; regular invocations take a slow IPC path into a Linux Driver Container, while a performance-critical Twin Driver in a Native Driver Container handles I/O IRQs directly on a fast path, keeping the control plane (init/wake) in the Linux container.
content.reading_order: Left to right: Apps and Device Manager feed the Virtual File System (via ioctl and registration), which redirects via IPC to the Linux Driver; a parallel fast path on the right lets Hardware IRQs reach the Twin Driver directly while control-plane calls (init/wake) still cross to the Linux Driver Container.

summary: This figure shows how HongMeng reuses Linux drivers while keeping critical I/O fast. A Device Manager registers a file node such as /dev/a in the Virtual File System for each driver; Apps invoke the driver through ioctl on that node, and the VFS redirects the call via IPC into a Linux Driver running inside a Linux Driver Container built on DC-Base. For performance-critical drivers, a Native Driver Container hosts a Twin Driver that receives Hardware I/O IRQs directly on a labeled 'Fast Path', while the corresponding control-plane operations (init/wake) still cross to the Linux Driver on a labeled 'Slow Path'. Circled numbers 1 through 5 tie each arrow to the registration, invocation, IPC redirection, control-plane synchronization, and fast-path IRQ delivery steps described in the text.
